summary: Build jem_notes on Flutter/Dart rather than Unity, React Native or Kotlin Multiplatform

options.description: Dart/Flutter — CustomPainter for staff+keyboard, flutter_notemus/simple_sheet_music for SMuFL, flutter_midi_pro for .sf2 piano audio (SELECTED)
React Native + Expo — best EAS/OTA delivery and reaches VexFlow/OSMD, but only via WebView latency on the core keyboard tap
Kotlin Multiplatform + Compose — right only if Kotlin is already daily; thinnest music ecosystem, most plumbing
Unity/C# — rejected; binary size and UI ergonomics paid up front for animation capability not needed

body:
## Problem statement

One codebase must ship to both App Store and Play Store. Core loop: draw a note
on a 5-line staff -> child taps a letter name -> child taps a piano key ->
feedback (likely with the note's sound). Trade-off axes: (1) dual-store delivery
friction, (2) custom 2D vector drawing + precise touch hit-testing (staff and
keyboard are both bespoke graphics, not stock widgets), (3) music-domain
ecosystem depth (SMuFL glyphs, soundfont audio), (4) solo-developer velocity in
one language, (5) growth path if the app becomes more game-like.

Floor independent of framework: iOS submission needs a Mac + $99/yr Apple
Developer Program membership regardless of choice.

## Options considered

- opt-flutter (SELECTED): Dart/Flutter. CustomPainter is the exact primitive for
  staff + keyboard with first-party hit-testing. Impeller is now the default
  Android renderer, so the historical first-run shader stutter is gone.
  Ecosystem already covers the domain: flutter_notemus and simple_sheet_music
  for SMuFL/Bravura engraving, flutter_midi_pro (.sf2 via FluidSynth on Android,
  AVFoundation on iOS) for real piano sound. Flame is the in-ecosystem escape
  hatch if gamification grows.
- opt-react-native: React Native + Expo. Best dual-store delivery (EAS, OTA
  updates) and unlocks the most mature notation engines in existence (VexFlow,
  OpenSheetMusicDisplay) - but those target DOM/SVG, so reaching them needs a
  WebView or a react-native-skia reimplementation.
- opt-kmp: Kotlin Multiplatform + Compose Multiplatform (iOS production-ready
  since May 2025). Right answer only if Kotlin is already the daily language;
  thinnest music-domain ecosystem and the most Gradle/Xcode plumbing for a solo
  project.
- opt-unity: Unity/C#. Rejected. Size overhead and painful text/UI work are paid
  up front for animation capability this app does not need. The operator's own
  instinct ("I don't think unity is necessary for a game of this simplicity")
  matched the industry rule of thumb: Flutter when an app is ~90% UI and ~10%
  gamification.

## Counter-argument to the selection

The strongest case against Flutter: the most mature music-notation rendering
code in existence is JavaScript (VexFlow, OpenSheetMusicDisplay, a decade of
engraving edge cases), and choosing Flutter cuts the project off from all of it,
forcing hand-drawn glyphs for a solved problem.

Rebuttal: engraving engines earn their complexity on multi-voice scores,
beaming, ties and slurs - none of which use case 1 contains. One note on five
lines plus a ledger line is a few hundred lines of CustomPainter, and Bravura is
an OFL-licensed font renderable directly. Meanwhile the React Native route to
those engines puts a WebView between the child's finger and the keyboard
hit-test, and instant tactile response on that keyboard is the one interaction
that must not feel laggy for a child.

Selected over opt-react-native because the notation-library advantage evaporates
at this app's complexity while the WebView latency cost lands on the core
interaction. Selected over opt-kmp because the music ecosystem is thinnest there
and the plumbing tax highest for a solo project. Selected over opt-unity because
a game engine's costs are all paid up front for capability this app lacks a use
for.

## Consequence

.github/workflows/ai-sdlc-gate.yml currently hardcodes a pnpm/Node toolchain
(pnpm install/lint/format:check/build/test/test:coverage) against a repo with no
package.json, so ai-sdlc/pr-ready fails unconditionally. This decision means
those jobs get rewritten for Flutter (flutter analyze / dart format --set-exit-if-changed
/ flutter test --coverage). The .husky/pre-push pnpm assumption and the CLAUDE.md
pre-commit checklist need the same treatment.

rationale: Operator selected Flutter/Dart after the decision-rubric walkthrough (problem statement, industry research, 4 options, recommendation + steel-manned counter-argument). App is ~90% UI with two bespoke 2D surfaces (staff, piano keyboard); CustomPainter plus the Bravura OFL font covers both, and flutter_midi_pro covers .sf2 piano audio. Counter-argument (VexFlow/OSMD maturity is JS-only) rejected because engraving engines earn their complexity on multi-voice scores this app does not render, while the WebView route would add latency to the one interaction that must feel instant to a child.

summary: Build and ship Android only for now; leave ios/ in the repo unbuilt

options.description: Android only — the learner practises on a Samsung A-series tablet; no Mac and no Apple Developer membership needed (SELECTED)
Build both from the start — needs a Mac plus $99/yr Apple Developer Program for a single known user on an Android tablet

body: The original framing asked for trivial delivery to both Android and iPhone, and DEC-0001 selected Flutter partly on that basis. The interview then established a single learner on a Samsung A-series tablet, sideloaded, with no intention to publish (RFC-0001 D10). iOS is therefore speculative today, and its build infrastructure carries real cost: a Mac for Xcode plus $99/yr for the Apple Developer Program. Flutter remains the right framework independently — it is also the strongest Android choice — so nothing about DEC-0001 changes. The ios/ directory stays in the repo, unbuilt, so re-enabling the target later is a CI change rather than a migration. Revisit if the app is ever shared beyond the family, which is also the trigger for revisiting the no-compliance posture in D10.

rationale: Single learner on an Android tablet, sideloaded, not published — iOS build infrastructure would cost a Mac plus $99/yr for a target nobody uses. Reversible: ios/ stays in the repo unbuilt, so re-enabling is a CI change.

summary: Drop the approving-review requirement on main; disarm auto-merge so the merge button is the review gate

options.description: Approvals to 0, auto-merge disarmed in both places — human gate is the deliberate merge click (SELECTED)
Give the agent a machine account so the maintainer's approval counts — Dependabot's shape; costs an account, PAT, changed authorship, second keyring entry
Approvals to 0 but keep auto-merge armed — anything green lands unseen; this is what happened to PR #3
Keep 1 required approval and bypass it as admin on every merge

body:
One human maintainer and one agent. GitHub forbids approving your own PR, and every PR is authored as the maintainer, so a 1-approval rule on main could only ever be satisfied by admin bypass (enforce_admins=false). Evidence: PR #1 and PR #2 both merged by rvodden with ZERO review records. A control that is always overridden is worse than no control, because it trains the operator to click through warnings — and this repo also carries DSSE attestations and a trusted-reviewer keyring where that habit matters.

Industry shape: single-maintainer repos protect main with required status checks and zero required reviews, because self-approval is impossible. The bot-authors/human-approves alternative is real and well-trodden (Dependabot, Renovate) and GitHub's Terms permit machine accounts, but it buys nothing while the maintainer reviews everything personally.

Counter-argument: dropping approvals while auto-merge stays armed is silently the fully-automatic option, and removes the only brake if the orchestrator is ever left to drain a backlog unattended. Addressed by disarming auto-merge in the same change — repo setting allow_auto_merge=false AND an if: vars.AI_SDLC_AUTO_MERGE == 'true' guard on the workflow, so both must be flipped to restore it. The brake becomes the maintainer's merge click. If autonomous operation is wanted later, that is the moment for opt-bot-identity, and it is cheap to add then.

Also kept required_status_checks strict with ai-sdlc/pr-ready, allow_force_pushes=false, allow_deletions=false. required_signatures remains off deliberately: turning it on would block the contents-API fallback used whenever 1Password is unreachable.

rationale: The maintainer IS the review — PR #2 was read and merged deliberately with no review record. Encoding that honestly beats a rule broken on every merge. Auto-merge disarmed in the same change so the click cannot be bypassed; revisit with a bot identity if agents ever merge unattended.

summary: Set AISDLC_REVIEW_STUB_AUTOPASS=true — the scaffolded review check passes without reviewing anything

options.description: Set the repo variable so the stub reports success (SELECTED)
Wire real reviewers into ai-sdlc-review.yml now — accurate signal, but the reviewers are subagents run locally, not in CI
Leave the stub failing — honest but makes every PR UNSTABLE, so the signal is ignored anyway

body:
ai-sdlc-review.yml ships as a STUB that fails closed: it posts 'Post Review Results' as a failure until either real reviewers replace the step or the repo variable AISDLC_REVIEW_STUB_AUTOPASS is set to true, which the workflow itself labels an acknowledged risk.

Context that makes autopass reasonable here: 'Post Review Results' is NOT a required status check (branch protection requires only ai-sdlc/pr-ready), so the red status never blocked anything — it only made every PR read as UNSTABLE, which trains the maintainer to ignore check colour. That is the same failure mode DEC-0003 addressed for the approval rule: a signal that is always overridden is worse than no signal.

WHAT THIS MEANS, recorded plainly so nobody is misled later: 'Post Review Results = SUCCESS' now certifies NOTHING. No review runs in CI. The actual review happens two other ways — the maintainer reading the PR before clicking merge (DEC-0003), and the reviewer subagents of /ai-sdlc execute, which run locally and write DSSE attestation verdicts to .ai-sdlc/verdicts/ rather than posting commit statuses.

Reversal trigger: if CI-side review is ever wired up, unset this variable in the same change, or the real result will be masked by the stub's success. Noted in the workflow's own comment at line 130.

rationale: The stub was not a required check, so its failure blocked nothing and only made every PR read UNSTABLE — colour that is always wrong gets ignored, the same trap DEC-0003 closed. Autopass makes the signal honest by being absent rather than false-negative. Risk accepted and recorded: the green check certifies nothing; review lives in the maintainer's merge click and in the local reviewer subagents' attestations.
